content: 1. Corticosteroids exhibit strong anti-inflammatory properties, although the exact mechanism by which they act on allergic rhinitis remains unclear. 2. Corticosteroids have been shown to exert effects on various cell types involved in inflammation, including mast cells, eosinophils, neutrophils, macrophages, and lymphocytes. They also influence inflammatory mediators such as histamine, eicosanoids, leukotrienes, and cytokines. 3. In two clinical studies using nasal antigen challenges, mometasone nasal spray (50 mcg) reduced markers of both earlyand late-phase allergic responses. These reductions included decreased histamine and eosinophil cationic protein levels (compared to placebo) and reductions in eosinophils, neutrophils, and epithelial cell adhesion proteins (compared to baseline). However, the clinical significance of these findings is not yet established. 4. A 12-month study involving 46 patients with allergic rhinitis examined the effects of mometasone nasal spray (50 mcg) on nasal mucosa. No evidence of atrophy was observed, and there was a significant reduction in intraepithelial eosinophilia and inflammatory cell infiltration, including eosinophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, neutrophils, and plasma cells. 5. Mometasone furoate monohydrate, the active ingredient in mometasone nasal spray (50 mcg), is a white powder with the chemical name 9,21-Dichloro-11ß,17-dihydroxy-16α-methylpregna-1,4-diene-3,20-dione 17-(2 furoate) monohydrate. Its empirical formula is C27H30Cl2O6·H2O, and its molecular weight is 539.45. 6. Mometasone furoate monohydrate is practically insoluble in water, slightly soluble in methanol, ethanol, and isopropanol, soluble in acetone and chloroform, and freely soluble in tetrahydrofuran. Its partition coefficient between octanol and water exceeds 5000. 7. Mometasone nasal spray (50 mcg) is a metered-dose, manual pump spray containing an aqueous suspension of mometasone furoate monohydrate equivalent to 0.05% w/w mometasone furoate (calculated on an anhydrous basis). The formulation includes glycerin, microcrystalline cellulose, carboxymethylcellulose sodium, sodium citrate, citric acid, benzalkonium chloride, and polysorbate 80, with a pH range of 4.3 to 4.9. 8. Four clinical pharmacology studies in adults assessed the effects of mometasone nasal spray (50 mcg) on adrenal function. In one study, daily doses of 200 mcg and 400 mcg of mometasone nasal spray were compared to 10 mg of prednisone and placebo in 64 patients with allergic rhinitis. Adrenal function was evaluated by measuring plasma cortisol levels after a 6-hour ACTH (Cortrosyn) infusion and 24-hour urinary free cortisol levels. 9. Mometasone nasal spray (50 mcg), at doses of 200 mcg and 400 mcg, did not result in statistically significant decreases in mean plasma cortisol levels post-Cortrosyn infusion or in 24-hour urinary free cortisol levels compared to placebo. In contrast, the prednisone group showed significant decreases in these parameters. 10. A second study evaluated adrenal response to mometasone nasal spray (400 mcg and 1600 mcg/day), prednisone (10 mg/day), and placebo over 29 days in 48 male volunteers. No statistically significant differences in adrenal function were observed with mometasone nasal spray compared to placebo. 11. A third study assessed single, rising doses of mometasone nasal spray (1000, 2000, and 4000 mcg/day), orally administered mometasone furoate (2000, 4000, and 8000 mcg/day), orally administered dexamethasone (200, 400, and 800 mcg/day), and placebo in 24 male volunteers. No significant decreases in cortisol levels were observed with mometasone treatments compared to placebo, whereas dexamethasone caused significant reductions. 12. A fourth study assessed adrenal function in 213 patients with nasal polyps treated with mometasone nasal spray (200 mcg once or twice daily) or placebo for 4 months. No significant decreases in 24-hour urinary free cortisol levels were observed with mometasone nasal spray compared to placebo. 13. Three pediatric studies evaluated the effects of mometasone furoate nasal spray on adrenal function. In one study, 48 children (ages 6 to 11) with allergic rhinitis were treated for 7 days with daily doses of 50, 100, or 200 mcg. No significant decreases in plasma cortisol or 24-hour urinary free cortisol levels were observed compared to placebo. 14. Mometasone nasal spray (50 mcg) at all doses did not result in significant decreases in cortisol levels compared to placebo. 15. In a third pediatric study, 52 children (ages 2 to 5) with allergic rhinitis were treated for up to 42 days with mometasone nasal spray (50 mcg per nostril, total daily dose 100 mcg). No significant decreases in plasma cortisol or 24-hour urinary free cortisol levels were observed compared to placebo. 16. Mometasone furoate nasal spray, when administered as a nasal spray suspension, has low systemic absorption.
